top_choice_rationale: P001 (Helpman and Melitz, B044) rests on a single originating model, Melitz 2003, that moved trade analysis from the industry to the firm and made selection and reallocation central to the gains from trade. The complementary Helpman-Melitz-Yeaple work on exporting versus foreign direct investment gives a separable second contribution. More than twenty years of firm-level evidence from many countries has confirmed the qualitative predictions. The disputes concern the size of welfare gains, not the mechanism, so a citation worded around selection, reallocation and the gains from trade is defensible. The main cost is that Bernard, Jensen, Eaton and Kortum, and arguably Redding, fall outside a two-name award, and the committee should say so openly. I place P002 (Autor, Hanson, Katz, B038) second. It is important, mature and transparent in its designs, but its credit boundary is less clear. The labour-demand work is arguably two strands, so the third name is a choice between Katz and Dorn, and the task framework has priority claims outside the ballot (Acemoglu, Levy, Murnane). The persistence of the China-shock effects is also still debated. I discount neither prize for adjacency to earlier prizes, because the earlier citations did not cover the same discoveries. The six-supporter count for P001 is a count of preferences and not evidence of merit. Both candidate prizes are clearly preferable to no award, so P000 is last.
recusal_note: none apparent from profile. No documented tie to Melitz, Helpman, Autor, Hanson, Katz or Dorn. I am a Lund colleague of Tommy Andersson. My research on local effects of railways and electrification is close in method to the local labour-market evidence in B038, which I treat as a reason for caution and not as evidence of merit.
